prize_parts.citation: for empirical and conceptual analyses of how technology and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: B018 combines three things I weigh together: new data and credible designs, an explanatory framework, and evidence that inspired follow-on work. The China-shock papers link commuting-zone labour-market outcomes to import exposure, and the task-based view of technology explains polarisation and wage inequality. This changed how economists and policymakers think about the local, distributional costs of trade and automation. The evidence is also unusually transparent and has been replicated, challenged and refined for over a decade, which shows maturity. Since my opening ranking I have moved from Katz to Dorn. The core China-shock papers are Autor-Dorn-Hanson, so that triple gives the cleanest attribution for a citation about trade and technology shocks to labour demand. Katz's major contribution is the long-run skill demand-and-supply framework, a related but separate line. That line also sits close to ground the Committee covered in 2023, so it is better treated as context than as a co-credit here.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The task-based framework has antecedents and parallel developers outside the credited list (Levy and Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo, Zeira), and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024. A citation resting on the China shock would be cleaner, but then it is an empirical-design contribution with a debated long-run interpretation. The shift-share identification, the persistence of effects and their magnitude are all still argued over. A three-person cap also forces me to leave out Katz, whose skill-premium work is foundational for the wider literature.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B018 seventh. He argued that the task-based theory behind the first strand is partly owed to people not credited here (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu), and that long-run follow-up is still accumulating and has qualified the effects.
responses.response: I accept the attribution point and have changed my proposal because of it. I no longer put Katz in the triple, and the citation is worded around technology and trade shocks to labour demand, not a task-theory discovery. I read the qualification of effects differently. Estimates of the China shock have been narrowed and extended by many independent users, which shows the contribution is durable and useful. I do agree that the task-framework credit is the weaker side, and I would not let the citation claim priority for the framework.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranked B018 fourth and put B001 and B050 above it. He flagged shift-share identification, the exposure designs, and the overlap of task-model credit with Acemoglu's work that the 2024 prize did not specifically cover.
responses.response: The shift-share concern is real, but it is a debate about the design that the authors and their critics have worked through openly, with new work on exposure designs and persistence. I count that as maturity rather than a flaw. On Acemoglu, the 2024 prize was about institutions and prosperity, so I do not read it as having covered the task framework. Even so, I would keep the citation anchored in the empirical evidence on labour demand and local labour markets so it does not claim ground that belongs to others. I also take his point on B001. Grossman-Helpman has the cleaner attribution and no identification dispute, and it is a serious alternative.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B018 second but proposed only Autor and Hanson. He said the set is crowded, the cut between Dorn and Katz is uncertain, and appetite may be affected by overlap with the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I agree the cut is the hard part. I would put Dorn ahead of Katz because the China-shock papers are a joint product of three authors. Taking Dorn out of the credit while rewarding that evidence would be hard to defend on attribution. Katz's work belongs to a different, earlier line, so I would not use him to fill the third slot for the same citation. I do not see why two names would be better than three. Dorn's role in the core papers is substantive, not marginal, and the citation reads cleanly with all three.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer Katz to Dorn if it frames the prize around the long-run skill-demand-and-supply framework rather than the China shock.
How far the long-run persistence and magnitude of trade-shock effects will hold up to continued re-estimation.
Whether a citation that blends the trade-shock and technology strands can be written as one coherent discovery, or whether the Committee would find it too broad.
How the task-framework credit to Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not on this ballot, should be handled.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I work in labour economics, so B018 is close to my own field, which I disclose as field proximity and not as a personal connection.
